title: Potato Gnocchi
subtitle: Italian potato dumplings with butter and sage
excerpt: Pillowy homemade potato gnocchi tossed in brown butter and sage. The dumplings require a light touch and the right potato: floury and dry, baked rather than boiled.

recipe.sourceNotes: Gnocchi (singular gnocco) are Italian dumplings made from potato, flour, and egg. They are one of the most widely eaten pasta-adjacent dishes in Italy, though they vary significantly from region to region: the Roman version (gnocchi alla romana) is made from semolina; Sardinian gnocchi (malloreddus) are made from semolina without potato; gnocchi di ricotta are made from ricotta and flour. The potato gnocchi eaten across northern Italy are the most internationally familiar. The technique is deceptively difficult: the right ratio of potato to flour determines the texture, and the potato variety and method of cooking it (baked, not boiled, to minimise moisture) determines the ratio. Too much flour makes the gnocchi dense and heavy; too little and they dissolve in the water. The test is to cook one gnocco in boiling water before shaping the rest: if it holds its shape and floats, the ratio is correct.

recipeTools.notes: A large saucepan for boiling the gnocchi. A frying pan for the butter and sage finish.

content.text: Bake the potatoes rather than boiling them: baking keeps the flesh dry, which means less flour is needed, which produces a lighter dumpling. Rice the potato while it is still very hot, spreading it on a board to let steam escape. Work the dough as little as possible once the flour and egg are added: overworking develops gluten and makes the gnocchi tough. The dough should be just cohesive enough to roll without falling apart. Dust the board and your hands lightly with flour and work quickly.

items.preparation: baked whole in their skins at 200 C for 1 hour; flesh scooped out and riced
plus extra for dusting; add gradually

content.text: Spread the riced potato on a board and leave to steam for 5 minutes. Season with salt. Make a well in the centre. Add the egg and half the flour. Gently fold together, adding more flour gradually until the dough just comes together. It should be soft but not sticky.

Divide the dough into 4 pieces. Roll each into a log about 2 cm thick on a lightly floured board. Cut into 2 cm pieces. To test: drop one gnocco into boiling salted water. If it holds together and floats after 2 minutes, the ratio is correct.

Cook the gnocchi in batches in well-salted boiling water for 2 to 3 minutes until they float. Meanwhile, melt the butter in a wide frying pan over medium heat until it turns golden-brown and smells nutty. Add the sage leaves and fry for 30 seconds. Lift the gnocchi from the water with a slotted spoon, add directly to the butter, and toss gently. Serve immediately with grated Parmesan.
